value_chain_position: Royalty/streaming layer - no operating or capex exposure, collects contractual metal-linked payment streams across a diversified portfolio; some non-metal energy royalties dilute the pure-gold mix.
cost_curve_verified: Direction agrees, magnitude disagrees: our deterministic screen reads a trailing operating margin of 97.8% (top-quartile of an eight-name cohort), while Franco-Nevada's own adjusted figure is 91.0% for the March 2026 quarter and 90.9% for full-year 2025 - the screen's version sweeps in one-off gains (the partial Cascabel stream buy-back, a Canada Revenue Agency refund, equity-sale gains) that the company excludes; the company-reported cash cost of $341 per gold-equivalent ounce in the March 2026 quarter (from $304 a year earlier, and $325 for full-year 2025 against $242 in 2020) confirms a far-left-of-the-cost-curve position at roughly a fifth of a typical gold producer's all-in sustaining cost.
gm_trajectory: Expanding on rising revenue: gross margin went from 71.0% in the March 2025 quarter ($261.5M on $368.4M) to 80.9% in the March 2026 quarter ($526.3M on $650.7M) while revenue grew 77% year over year - the cost per gold-equivalent ounce is near-fixed, so the metal price converts almost dollar-for-dollar into profit; margin per ounce roughly doubled from over $2,500 (March 2025 quarter) to about $4,159 (March 2026 quarter).
bull_thesis: Franco-Nevada is the highest-quality asset in the precious-metals complex and the market is currently pricing it as though the last eighteen months of portfolio building never happened. Three things carry the case. First, the cost structure is close to unassailable. The company collects a slice of metal from 121 producing mines it does not operate, at a cash cost of $341 per gold-equivalent ounce against a typical producer's all-in sustaining cost near $1,600-1,800. That means margin per ounce roughly doubled over five quarters, from over $2,500 in the March 2025 quarter to about $4,159 in the March 2026 quarter, and gross margin widened from 71.0% to 80.9% on revenue up 77% year over year. No cost-inflation question exists here because there is no cost base to inflate - management stated it plainly in the May 2025 call: 'in a rising commodity price environment, we expect to benefit fully as the cost per GEO should not increase significantly.' The record verifies the claim. Second, the balance sheet and the ownership record are exceptional for this sector. Total debt is zero, cash and short-term investments are $717M as of 31 March 2026, and the diluted share count went from 192.5 million to 193.2 million across eight quarters - growth of roughly 0.5% - while the company funded ten major acquisitions. Every deal came from cash flow or a revolver repaid inside a quarter. The dividend has risen for nineteen consecutive years, most recently by 16% in January 2026, and management refused a special dividend twice when analysts pressed for one. That is the opposite of the sector's usual pattern of issuing stock into every rally. Third, there are two free options attached that cost nothing to hold. Cobre Panama was fully written off at the 2023 shutdown and has never appeared in guidance - as management put it in the August 2025 call, 'it's all upside to us... we're not dependent on it in any way.' The path since has been one-directional: the operator withdrew its international arbitration in March 2026, Panama authorised stockpile processing and export in April 2026, and the government-commissioned environmental audit released in June 2026 scored the mine 88% and found it broadly compliant. Panama's Commerce Minister has said the government expects to decide among its options by the end of 2026. A restart, at today's copper price of $6.65 a pound and gold at $4,155, would add something like $480M of revenue at near-100% margin. The second free option is the resource base itself: measured and indicated resources support 34 years of mining at current rates, with inferred resources adding another 12, across a portfolio covering roughly 70,000 square kilometres of mineral rights. Rising metal prices push lower-grade material into mine plans at zero cost to Franco-Nevada - the mechanism management sketched in the November 2025 call, where a higher reserve price assumption alone moves large tonnages into the plan. For this case to work, three conditions must hold: gold must stabilise at or above roughly $4,150 rather than continuing its slide from the March peak of $5,366; the Cobre Panama negotiation must reach a restart rather than a state-owned-company outcome that strands the stream; and management must stop paying full prices for new royalties or, at minimum, keep the acquired cost per ounce near the $770 average it has claimed for its most recent 820,000 ounces.
bear_thesis: The bear case does not require anything to break. It only requires the metal to keep doing what it has already been doing for five months, and it requires an honest look at what the growth headline actually contains. Start with the price of gold, because at a two-year beta of 1.02 to the metal this is close to the whole story. Gold peaked at $5,366 an ounce on 1 March 2026 and trades at $4,155 today - down 22.6%. Franco-Nevada peaked at $285.67 and trades at $221.30 - down 22.5%. The stock has tracked the metal essentially one-for-one, which means the multiple has not compressed at all; it has quietly expanded as earnings fell. The record March 2026 quarter - $650.7M of revenue, $591.9M of adjusted operating profit - was earned at an average gold price around $4,880. The June quarter averaged roughly $4,510 and the September quarter is averaging roughly $4,095 so far. Applying the portfolio's own symmetric torque, where a 10% move in the commodity swings operating profit by about 8.2%, the 15% decline from the March-quarter average to today's spot takes roughly 12-13% out of operating profit before anything else happens. On a spot deck the run-rate is closer to $2.0 billion of operating profit than the $2.06 billion trailing figure, and well short of the $2.37 billion the March quarter annualises to. The market is paying about 21 times enterprise value to operating profit for a number that is shrinking. Second, strip Cobre Panama out and the organic growth is thin. Management called this 'the most exciting growth outlook in the space' in the August 2025 call and pointed to 'roughly 50% growth in GEOs over 5 years.' The published 2030 outlook excluding a Cobre restart is 555,000-615,000 gold-equivalent ounces, against 519,106 delivered in 2025. That is 7% to 18% over five years - roughly 1.5% to 3.5% a year. Almost the entire growth headline is a Panamanian political decision plus the metal price. Third, capital is being deployed at exactly the wrong point in the cycle by management's own framework. In the August 2025 call Paul Brink said: 'you do want to have a gut sense of where you are in the cycle... Where do you want to spend a lot of money - that's at the bottom of the cycle.' The company then spent through the highest gold prices in recorded history: six major acquisitions in eighteen months, four more in the March 2026 quarter alone. Return on invested capital of 14.3% now trails Wheaton Precious Metals at 18.1% - the arithmetic signature of paying up. If gold reverts, those contracts were bought at prices that will look very different. Fourth, and newest, the enforceability of the contract book is no longer theoretical. On 10 June 2026 the Commercial Court of Ouagadougou nullified the 2014 gold purchase agreement covering the Karma mine in Burkina Faso and ordered Franco-Nevada to pay roughly $9.3 million to the operator. The company's position, stated on 16 June 2026, is that the agreement is governed by Ontario law and the judgment is invalid, and it is pursuing remedies in Ontario and elsewhere. The dollars at stake are immaterial. The precedent is not: the entire premise of a royalty company is that a contract binds regardless of who governs the country, and one court has now held otherwise. Peru, Chile, South Africa, Ecuador, Panama and Argentina all carry material assets. Fifth, two smaller erosions. The oil royalty book that management flagged in May 2026 as a coming tailwind - crude 'hovering around $100 per barrel' after the late-February Iran events - has already given the gain back; West Texas Intermediate trades at $75.74 today, essentially at the $70 guidance assumption. And the $1.33 billion long-term investment portfolio, marked at 31 March 2026 near the top of the junior-mining tape, carries $506 million of unrealised gains that will mark down with the sector. What confirms the bear case: a September-quarter print that shows revenue falling sequentially from $650.7M; a Panamanian decision that routes the mine to a state-owned entity rather than a restart under the existing operator; and any further host-country judgment against a stream contract.
sop_bull: Favourable sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately), assuming gold holds at $4,500 an ounce - the company's own 2026 conversion price - crude at $85, Cobre Panama restarting, and the multiple re-expanding to reflect scarcity value: $266 per share. Parts: (1) the precious-metals royalty and stream book, about $2,093M of revenue on roughly 465,000 precious-metal ounces less about $175M of cash cost and $47M of allocated overhead, so about $1,871M of operating profit, at 23 times = $43.03B - a premium to Wheaton Precious Metals' 21 times, justified by the largest and most diversified producing portfolio in the sector, zero debt and 34 years of measured-and-indicated reserve life; (2) the oil and gas royalty book, about $235M of revenue at near-100% margin, at 11 times = $2.59B; (3) other diversified royalties (the Vale iron-ore royalty, copper and platinum-group byproduct), about $85M of operating profit at 12 times = $1.02B; (4) net cash of $717M as of 31 March 2026; (5) the marketable investment portfolio, carried at $1,335M at 31 March 2026, taken at $1,200M; (6) the Cobre Panama restart option, valued at a restarted stream worth roughly $380M of annual operating profit capitalised at 12 times = $4.6B, weighted 70% for probability and 0.9 for timing = $2.90B. Total $51.45B over 193.2 million diluted shares = $266.
sop_bear: Adverse sum-of-the-parts, assuming the precious-metals cycle turns against the name - gold reverting to $3,500 an ounce (still far above the 2025 average of roughly $3,300), crude back to $60, no Cobre Panama restart, and the sector multiple de-rating toward where Triple Flag and Royal Gold trade today: $132 per share. Parts: (1) the precious-metals book, about $1,628M of revenue less roughly $175M of cash cost and $47M of overhead, so about $1,443M of operating profit, at 16 times = $23.09B - note that this de-rating is the larger driver of the loss, not the metal itself, because the near-fixed cost base means the portfolio's own symmetric torque only takes about 8.2% out of operating profit per 10% decline in the commodity; (2) the oil and gas royalties at $60 crude, about $150M of operating profit at 7 times = $1.05B; (3) other diversified royalties, about $55M at 8 times = $0.44B; (4) net cash $717M; (5) the investment portfolio marked down with the junior-mining tape from $1,335M to $600M; (6) Cobre Panama at zero - the mine stays shut or is routed to a state-owned entity that strands the stream; (7) a $300M discount applied across the non-OECD contract book to price the enforceability risk the Burkina Faso judgment of 10 June 2026 demonstrated. Total $25.60B over 193.2 million diluted shares = $132, about 41% below today's $221.30.
sop_fair_value: $205 per share (base case, on today's spot deck of $4,155 gold, $60 silver and $75.74 crude), against a live price of $221.30 - the shares trade at a modest premium to what the parts support.
sop_breakdown: (1) Precious-metals royalty and stream book - about 85% of revenue. On a spot deck of $4,155 gold and $60 silver, roughly 465,000 precious-metal gold-equivalent ounces produce about $1,910M of revenue; deducting about $175M of cash cost (at $341 per ounce) and about $47M of allocated overhead leaves roughly $1,688M of operating profit. Valued at 20 times enterprise value to operating profit = $33.76B. That multiple sits between Wheaton Precious Metals at 21.0 times and Royal Gold at 17.4 times, and is justified by Franco-Nevada's scale, zero debt and 34 years of measured-and-indicated reserve life. (2) Oil and gas royalties - about 11% of revenue. Roughly $215M of revenue at near-100% margin, so about $200M of operating profit, at 9 times = $1.80B. These are non-operated, capex-free, long-life interests but they deserve an energy multiple, not a gold one. (3) Other diversified royalties - about 4% of revenue, principally the Vale iron-ore royalty plus copper and platinum-group byproduct: about $70M of operating profit at 10 times = $0.70B. (4) Net cash: $717M as of 31 March 2026, with zero total debt - a genuine add-back, worth $3.71 per share. (5) Marketable investment portfolio: carried at $1,335M at 31 March 2026, including $506M of unrealised gains booked to other comprehensive income; haircut to $900M for the junior-mining drawdown since that mark. (6) Cobre Panama restart option: a restarted precious-metals stream is worth roughly $380M of annual operating profit at today's metal prices, capitalised at 12 times for restart risk = $4.6B, weighted 45% for probability and 0.85 for timing = $1.76B, or about $9 per share. Carried at zero on the company's books since the 2023 write-off. Total $39.64B over 193.2 million diluted shares = about $205. A useful cross-check on the segment weights: the deterministic segment feed reads Mining $1.82B at 34%, but $1.82B is in fact the whole of 2025 revenue, not a segment - the percentages in that feed are computed against a double-counted denominator. The company's own split is 85% precious metals, 11% energy, 4% other, which is what this breakdown uses.
risk_reward: Unfavourable at today's price. The shares trade at $221.30 against a base-case parts value of $205 - so there is no upside to fair value; you are paying about 8% above what the parts support. The adverse case, which requires only that gold revert to $3,500 (still above the 2025 average) with no Cobre Panama restart and a sector de-rating to 16 times, prices at $132. The favourable case, which requires gold to hold $4,500 and Cobre to restart, prices at $266. Downside to the adverse case is $89.30 a share; upside to the favourable case is $44.70. The Street's $280 consensus target sits above even the favourable case's $266 and requires peak metal prices, a peak multiple and a Cobre restart simultaneously.
catalyst_status_note: The load-bearing event is the Cobre Panama restart decision, and it is a soft, non-binding catalyst controlled by a third party - Panama's government - with a stated but repeatedly moved target date. The dated record: the operator withdrew its international arbitration against Panama in March 2026; Panama authorised processing and export of on-site stockpiles in April 2026; the government-commissioned environmental audit was released around 22 June 2026 with an overall compliance score of 88%; Panama's Commerce and Industry Minister Julio Molto has said the government expects to decide among its options by the end of 2026. That target has already slipped once - on the 4 November 2025 call management described end-2025 as President Mulino's stated objective. Options reportedly under consideration include a state-owned vehicle and a materially higher tax and royalty burden, either of which could change what a restart is worth to Franco-Nevada. Note for the record that this status is descriptive only and does not drive the verdict here: the dated-event book is handled elsewhere, and this lane judges the operating and value case. A separate hard date exists - second-quarter 2026 results are scheduled for 12 August 2026 after market close - but a scheduled earnings release is not a thesis catalyst.
peer_comps_note: Against the assigned competitor set, Franco-Nevada is priced at the top of the quality tier rather than at a discount to it. On enterprise value to trailing operating profit: Franco-Nevada 20.6 times, Wheaton Precious Metals 21.0 times, Royal Gold 17.4 times, Triple Flag 15.1 times. Sandstorm at 46.4 times is not a usable comparison - it carries net debt of 3.7 times operating profit and a return on equity of 1.8%, so its multiple reflects distress rather than quality. Osisko Gold Royalties and Metalla are materially smaller. On quality Franco-Nevada earns its place: return on equity 18.7%, return on invested capital 14.3%, net cash of 0.19 times operating profit, and the best margin in the group. But two comparisons matter for sizing. Wheaton, at a nearly identical multiple, earns a higher return on invested capital (18.1% versus 14.3%) and carries more net cash (0.90 times operating profit versus 0.19), which is what deploying more than $4 billion into a record-price tape looks like on the ledger. And Royal Gold and Triple Flag at 17.4 and 15.1 times set the floor the sector de-rates toward when the metal falls - the reference points used in the adverse case. The base-case 20 times applied to the precious-metals book therefore sits at a deliberate premium to the median of the set, which the scale and diversification support but do not make cheap.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is on the direction of the disagreement itself. This is not a case where the Street is too bearish and we see hidden value; it is one where the Street is extrapolating a peak and we do not. The consensus target is $280 with a median of $282.50, implying about 27% upside from $221.30, and the recent individual targets cluster tightly around it: RBC Capital at $285 on 9 July 2026, Daniel Major at $280 on 30 June 2026, TD Securities at $291 on 20 May 2026, Tanya Jakusconek at $274 on 14 July 2026. Only Jefferies at $245, dated 6 July 2026, is anywhere near our base-case parts value of $205. Three specific assumptions inside those targets are, in our reading, wrong. First, most of these targets carry forward an earnings base built at a gold price that no longer exists. The record March 2026 quarter was earned at an average gold price around $4,880 an ounce. Gold trades at $4,155 today - the June quarter averaged roughly $4,510 and the September quarter is averaging roughly $4,095 so far. Applying the portfolio's own symmetric torque, where a 10% commodity move swings operating profit by about 8.2%, that path removes roughly 12-13% from operating profit before anything else changes. A $280 target on a shrinking denominator implies a multiple above 24 times operating profit - a level normally reserved for trough earnings, not peak ones. Second, the Street is treating the growth outlook as a company attribute when it is mostly a Panamanian political outcome. The headline of roughly 45-50% production growth to 2030 that appears in most notes is contingent on a Cobre Panama restart. The published outlook excluding Cobre is 555,000-615,000 gold-equivalent ounces in 2030 against 519,106 delivered in 2025 - between 7% and 18% over five years, or roughly 1.5% to 3.5% a year. If you strip the political option out of the growth line, you are left with a very slow-growing, very high-quality annuity, which is worth a fine multiple but not an expanding one. Third, almost nobody is pricing enforcement risk on the contract book. The Commercial Court of Ouagadougou nullified the 2014 Karma gold purchase agreement on 10 June 2026 and ordered a roughly $9.3 million payment to the operator. The dollars are trivial; the precedent is not, because the premise of every royalty valuation is that an Ontario-law contract binds regardless of who governs the ground it sits on. Peru, Chile, South Africa, Ecuador, Panama and Argentina all carry material assets. Not one recent target we can see applies a jurisdictional discount to that book. The honest summary: the market and we agree this is the best business in the sector. We disagree that a 27% gain is available from a full multiple on falling earnings.
valley_of_death: There is no cash-burn hump, no maturity wall and no financing risk here - total debt is zero, cash and short-term investments are $717M, undrawn revolver capacity is $2.25B ($1.5B at the parent plus $750M at the Barbados subsidiary), and free cash flow is running at about $1.78B a year. The company could not get into trouble on its balance sheet if it tried. The risk over the next three to nine months is entirely to the reported earnings line and to sentiment, and it is mechanical rather than speculative. Three things land in that window. First, and largest, the earnings reset. The March 2026 quarter set a record at $650.7M of revenue on a gold price averaging around $4,880. The June quarter averaged roughly $4,510, and the September quarter is averaging roughly $4,095. Second-quarter results are due 12 August 2026 after market close, and third-quarter results in early November. Both are likely to show revenue falling sequentially from the record - the first sequential declines in six quarters. For a stock whose entire narrative for eighteen months has been 'the third time this year we're announcing record quarterly results,' a broken record streak is a sentiment event out of proportion to its economic significance. Second, the oil give-back. Management told the market on 13 May 2026 that West Texas Intermediate crude 'hovering around $100 per barrel' would 'positively impact our energy revenue for Q2,' with an explicit sensitivity of roughly 12% more oil revenue per $10 above the $70 guidance assumption. Crude trades at $75.74 today. The June quarter will capture part of that windfall; the September quarter will not. Anyone who marked up their model on the May guidance will be marking it back down. Third, the investment portfolio marks down. The $1,335M long-term investment book was struck at 31 March 2026, when gold was at $4,679 and junior mining equities were near their highs. It carries $506M of unrealised gains. Those gains flow through other comprehensive income rather than earnings, so they will not hit reported per-share profit, but they will reduce book value and they will be visible. Two lower-probability items sit in the same window. Panama could route Cobre to a state-owned vehicle rather than a restart under the existing operator, which would move that option from partly-valued to zero. And a further adverse judgment in the Burkina Faso matter, or a similar action elsewhere, would force the market to apply a jurisdictional discount it currently does not apply. Neither is likely to be resolved before year-end.
positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling mechanism available here, and that is itself part of the risk - the shares are unlikely to be handed to you cheaply by a mechanical seller. The dividend is not at risk in any scenario we can construct: it has risen for nineteen consecutive years, was raised 16% in January 2026, and consumes a small fraction of $1.78B of free cash flow. Management has twice refused calls for a special dividend, most recently in the May 2026 call - 'I don't think you'll see any sort of special dividend coming from Franco.' No income-oriented holder will be forced out. There is no leverage, so no covenant or margin dynamic exists. The shareholder base is instead dominated by two groups whose selling is gradual rather than mechanical. The first is passive and generalist - gold and materials index funds, and institutions like Bank of Nova Scotia, which added 23,587 shares in the March quarter. Passive holders sell only when the index weight falls, which happens smoothly as the price falls, not in a cascade. The second is the 'quality gold proxy' allocation: investors who own Franco-Nevada specifically because they want gold exposure without operational risk. That group's exit is the one to watch, and it is behavioural rather than forced. It happens when the metal has fallen far enough for long enough that the whole precious-metals sleeve is cut, which typically requires a multi-quarter downtrend rather than a single shock. Gold is five months into a decline from its 1 March 2026 peak. The practical read: expect a slow bleed rather than a flush. A genuine capitulation print would need gold to break decisively below roughly $3,800 an ounce, which would likely take the shares toward the 52-week low of $164.91 and into the range where the parts value supports a purchase with a real margin of safety. Absent that, patience is the position.
forcing_function: Two dated events could reprice the shares, and one undated structural one. The nearer and more certain is second-quarter 2026 results on 12 August 2026 after market close, with a call the following morning. This is a re-rating event in the ordinary sense rather than a thesis-breaker: it will show the first sequential revenue decline in six quarters, it will contain management's updated commentary on the oil royalty book after crude round-tripped from roughly $100 in mid-May to $75.74 today, and it should carry the first substantive update on both the Burkina Faso litigation and the Cobre Panama audit's final report. It reframes the earnings base rather than changing the business. The larger one is the Panamanian government's decision on Cobre Panama, which Commerce and Industry Minister Julio Molto has indicated the government expects to make by the end of 2026. This is genuinely binary and it is worth roughly $9 a share in our base case, more if the terms are favourable and nothing if the mine is routed to a state-owned entity. It is not, however, in Franco-Nevada's control, and the timeline has already slipped once from the end-2025 objective President Mulino stated in late 2025. Treat it as a real possibility with an unreliable date, not as a scheduled payout. The undated structural item is the one that actually determines the outcome and has no event attached: the gold price itself. With a two-year beta to the metal of 1.02, this position is a leveraged, slightly-better-than-one-for-one expression of a view on gold with an exceptional business attached. Nothing forces a re-rating independent of the metal. That is precisely why the discipline here is a price level rather than a date.
moderator_conclusion: Franco-Nevada is the best business in its sector and it is not cheap. Both halves of that sentence matter, and the second one decides the call. Take the quality first, because it is real and it survives every test we ran. The company collects contractual slices of metal from 121 producing mines it does not operate, at a cash cost of $341 per gold-equivalent ounce against a typical producer's all-in sustaining cost near $1,600-1,800. That is not an operating advantage, it is a structural one, and it shows up exactly where it should: gross margin widened from 71.0% to 80.9% over the year to March 2026 while revenue grew 77%, and margin per ounce roughly doubled. Measured and indicated resources support 34 years of mining at current rates, with inferred adding another 12. Total debt is zero, cash is $717M, and the diluted share count grew about 0.5% across eight quarters while the company funded ten major acquisitions - in a sector whose defining sin is issuing stock into every rally, that record is close to unique. Guidance for 2025 was met at the top of its range. The dividend has risen nineteen years running and management refused a special dividend twice under direct analyst pressure. On the forensic record we score management a 4 out of 5, with the trajectory strengthening. Now the price. The record March 2026 quarter was earned at an average gold price around $4,880 an ounce. Gold trades at $4,155 today, roughly 22.6% below its 1 March 2026 peak of $5,366. The shares are down 22.5% from their high over the same stretch - almost exactly one-for-one, which is what a two-year beta of 1.02 predicts, and which means the multiple has not compressed at all. It has quietly expanded as the earnings underneath it fell. Applying the portfolio's own symmetric torque - a 10% commodity move swings operating profit by about 8.2%, and that cuts both ways - the move from the March-quarter average to today's spot removes roughly 12-13% of operating profit before anything else happens. Valuing the business by its parts on today's spot deck gives us about $205 a share: the precious-metals book at 20 times, between Wheaton at 21.0 and Royal Gold at 17.4; the oil and gas royalties at 9 times; other diversified at 10 times; plus net cash, a marked-down investment portfolio, and about $9 a share for a probability-weighted Cobre Panama restart. The shares trade at $221.30. There is no discount to capture. Three specific things keep us from a higher score. The growth headline is mostly a Panamanian political outcome: strip Cobre out and the published 2030 outlook of 555,000-615,000 ounces against 519,106 delivered in 2025 is 1.5% to 3.5% a year. Capital is being deployed at what management's own stated framework calls the wrong half of the cycle - Paul Brink said in August 2025 that you want to spend heavily at the bottom, and the company then spent through the highest gold prices in history; return on invested capital of 14.3% against Wheaton's 18.1% is the ledger's signature of paying up. And the enforceability of the contract book stopped being theoretical on 10 June 2026, when a Burkinabe court nullified a 2014 stream agreement and ordered a $9.3 million payment. The dollars are trivial; the precedent is not, and a meaningful share of the portfolio sits in jurisdictions where it could matter. On the other side, we credit the discipline: Cobre was fully written off in 2023, has never appeared in guidance, and management has consistently called it upside rather than a base case. That restraint is why the option is worth something rather than nothing. Two promotional tells are worth naming so a reader is not misled by them - the $124 billion attributable-ounce figure set beside the market value in May 2026 is a gross, undiscounted, un-permitted count that includes inferred ounces, and quoting two-week share-price gains on junior equity stakes is momentum, not underwriting. The call is to wait, with a named level. Our base-case parts value is $205. A 20% margin of safety against that is roughly $162 - essentially the 52-week low of $164.91, which is where a genuine gold-sector capitulation would likely put the shares and where the risk and reward would invert in our favour. Below roughly $175 this becomes a straightforward purchase of a wide-moat, debt-free, top-of-cost-curve franchise at a discount. At $221.30 you are paying above what the parts support, on an earnings base a falling metal price is already eroding, for a business that grows in low single digits without a political decision going its way. The Street's $280 target sits above even our favourable $266 case and requires peak gold, a peak multiple and a Cobre restart at once. This is a name to own, at a price we do not have yet.
